newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa protests over Nigerian jibe.
newsitem.headline: South Africa protests over Nigerian jibe.

text.p: South Africa's ruling ANC lashed out on Monday over a perceived Nigerian slur on President Nelson Mandela's leadership after a government minister called him the black head of a white country.

But Mandela's office said the diplomatic row would not deter South African initiatives to promote democracy on the continent, nor distract Mandela from talks with Nigeria's military ruler Sani Abacha.
South African media this weekend quoted Information Minister Walter Ofonagoro as telling a forum of the Nigerian Guild of Editors that "South Africa is at the centre of anti-Nigerian propaganda".
"South Africa is a white country with a black head of state," he added.
Mandela's African National Congress, which took power in the country's first all-race poll in 1994, said in a statement it had noted the remarks with "shock and disgust".

"The comments not only slight the integrity, name and reputation of our beloved President Nelson Mandela, but also offend the entire South African nation," said Ronnie Mamoepa, the spokesman for the ruling party.

Presidential spokesman Joel Netshitenzhe said in a separate statement that Mandela was eagerly awaiting a reply from Nigeria to a note of protest delivered by South Africa's High Commission in Lagos to the Nigerian foreign ministry.
"If true...the statement is both unfortunate and ill-informed," Netshitenzhe said.

"However, President Mandela does not wish (it) to detract from the sensitive initiative that he and the leader of the Nigerian government have been engaged in with regard to some of the conflict on the continent.
"Neither should it subtract from the challenges Nigeria faces with regard to democratisation and human rights," he said.
Abacha, who seized power during chaos unleashed when his army predecessor annulled a 1993 presidential poll, has promised to hand over to an elected government in October next year.
